summary:
Earth science data is predominantly communicated through complex visual color maps, leaving millions of individuals who are blind or have low vision (BLV) locked out of critical environmental insights. Earth Information Jukebox bridges this accessibility gap by transforming NASA visualizations into an interactive, multi-modal auditory experience.

Using canvas-based pixel scanning and Tone.js synthesis, the application converts visual color intensities into real-time spatial audio pitches. Users can independently explore datasets, such as GEOS-CF carbon monoxide or VIIRS active fires, through three distinct navigation modes: continents, oceans, and map grids.

By mimicking how sighted users read maps, our solution empowers BLV students, researchers, and citizens to orient themselves by ear, experience exact data values through color-to-audio intensity mapping, and independently engage with the same vital science shaping our changing planet.
details:
Project Details

The Human Story & The Pain Point

Earth science tells the story of our changing planet through rich visual maps and satellite imagery. But for the 295 million people worldwide with moderate or severe distance vision impairment, including BLV students and researchers, those maps are locked behind an invisible wall.

Currently, a color scale means nothing to a screen reader. While basic alt-text can offer a brief overview, it forces researchers and students to be entirely dependent on summaries generated by others. They cannot independently explore where pollution peaks, how a wildfire spreads across a region, or investigate the data themselves. This bottleneck compromises true scientific autonomy and shuts eager minds out of critical environmental evidence.

What Our Solution Does & How It Works

Earth Information Jukebox bridges this gap by transforming NASA Earth visualizations into an intuitive, accessible auditory experience. Instead of relying on someone else's description, users can explore maps directly using a keyboard and screen reader.

The application works through three core layers:

  1. Direct Canvas Pixel Scanning: Instantly inspects pixel color data and scientific values in real-time.
  2. Spatial Audio Synthesis: Powered by Tone.js using smooth triangle waves, colors map directly into pitch, low values play low notes, and high values rise, letting users feel exact data intensity and environmental shifts by ear.
  3. Three Navigation Types: Mimicking how sighted users read maps, users can orient themselves and navigate through three structured forms: Oceans (basin-by-basin), Continents (regional boundary sweeps), and Grids (precise multi-zone tracking). Users always know their exact location on the map.

User Experience, Accessibility & Impact

Built strictly with WCAG guidelines, ARIA landmarks and User Experience (UX) in mind, every interaction is fully screen-reader friendly. The impact is transformative: it replaces dependency with independence. Blind and low-vision researchers, students, and citizens can finally explore complex NASA datasets on their own terms, gaining the same spatial awareness and analytical freedom that sighted users take for granted.

Github link: https://github.com/unnatimistry-uxr/NASA_earth_information_jukebox.git

Tech Stack & Tools Used

  • Languages & Core Logic: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (Canvas API for pixel scanning, requestAnimationFrame for smooth cursor movement).
  • Audio & Accessibility Engine: Tone.js (for triangular wave audio synthesis), ARIA live regions, and semantic landmarks.
  • Data Sources: Official NASA resources and datasets (such as GEOS-CF carbon monoxide and VIIRS active fires).
